planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Masquerade, bred by Eugene S. Boerner and introduced by Jackson & Perkins in 1949, won the RNRS Gold Medal in the UK in 1952 and is one of the most famous color-changing floribundas ever bred.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Masquerade bears clustered double flowers that open yellow, shift to orange-pink, and deepen to red as they age, so a single spray often displays all three colors at once. This tricolor, mood-ring effect made it one of the most widely planted and talked-about floribundas of the mid-20th century and an influential parent in later color-changing rose breeding, including the Explorer-series climber 'John Cabot'. It is a vigorous, upright grower well suited to beds and borders where its shifting color display can be appreciated up close. A preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates, and deadheading spent clusters keeps the color show coming.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Allgold, bred by Edward LeGrice and introduced in Britain in 1956, won the RNRS Gold Medal and was valued for holding its deep yellow color without fading or pinking with age.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Allgold bears clusters of double, deep golden-yellow flowers over small, glossy dark green foliage on a compact, bushy plant. Unlike many yellow roses of its era that faded or pinked with age and sun exposure, Allgold was prized for holding a clean, saturated gold color from bud to drop, making it a dependable choice for color-focused beds and low borders. A preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom, and prune moderately in late winter.

common_name: Gene Boerner Rose (Tall Pink Exhibition Floribunda)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gene Boerner, introduced by Jackson & Perkins in 1968 and named for the influential hybridizer behind many classic floribundas, won the AARS award in 1969.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gene Boerner bears high-centered, double, clear medium-pink flowers with an almost hybrid-tea quality of form, carried in clusters on unusually long, strong stems for a floribunda. Its tall, upright habit and elegant flower form have made it a favorite for cutting as well as garden display, bridging the gap between floribunda profusion and hybrid-tea refinement. A preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom, and prune moderately in late winter.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sarabande, bred by Francis Meilland in France in 1957 and winner of the AARS award in 1960, is valued for its exceptionally vivid, nonstop orange-red bloom.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sarabande bears semi-double, vivid orange-red flowers with prominent golden stamens, held in large trusses on a low, dense, spreading plant that blooms with unusual persistence from late spring to frost. Its saturated, fire-engine color and compact habit have made it a long-standing favorite for mass bedding displays where continuous, high-impact color matters most. A preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent clusters to sustain heavy repeat bloom, and prune moderately in late winter.

common_name: Elizabeth of Glamis Rose (Fragrant Salmon-Orange Floribunda)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Elizabeth of Glamis, bred by Sam McGredy and introduced in 1963, is also sold as 'Irish Beauty' and is noted for its strong fragrance among roses of its class.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Elizabeth of Glamis bears double, salmon-orange to coral-pink flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance unusual for a floribunda of its generation, carried in generous clusters on a bushy, well-rounded plant. Its combination of fragrance, warm coloring, and reliable repeat bloom made it a standout garden rose in its era and a continuing favorite where scent is a priority. A preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom, and prune moderately in late winter.

planting.note: Transplant nursery starts after all danger of frost into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; in cold climates grow in containers and overwinter under cover.

directions: This Spanish lavender selection is grown for its unusually large, wide upper bracts that flare outward above each dense flower cone, giving the bloom spike a distinctive butterfly-wing silhouette compared to the narrower bracts of most stoechas cultivars. Like other Spanish lavenders it blooms earlier in spring than English types and often repeats through the season on a compact, rounded plant. It is less cold-hardy than English lavender and dislikes humid summers or heavy, wet soil, so gardeners outside its comfort zone often grow it in containers that can be sheltered over winter. Give it full sun, lean well-drained soil, and minimal supplemental water once established, deadheading spent spikes to encourage repeat bloom.
